title: q-series, partition statistics and mock modular forms
summary: Finite and formal q-calculus, partition identities and congruences, and the analytic completion theory of Appell–Lerch sums, signature-(r−1,1) theta series and meromorphic Jacobi coefficients, ending in harmonic weak Maass forms and explicit mock theta and rank transformations.

layers.title: finite, integer-indexed and formal q-products

targets.name: qPochhammerFin
targets.statement: For a commutative ring K, a,q∈K and n∈ℕ, define Pₙ(a;q)=∏_{j<n}(1−a qʲ). A finite parameter list means the product with multiplicity, including the empty list.
hypotheses: K commutative unital ring; n≥0; no domain or characteristic condition

locator.where: (1.2.3), p. 2, line 81; list notation (2.1.7), p. 9, line 477; Gasper1995 line 81

Positive indices use Pₙ and need no unit hypotheses on their factors. The negative-index domain is explicit.
hypotheses: q∈Kˣ; for index −n each factor 1−a q^(−j) is a unit for 1≤j≤n

targets.name: qPochhammerRatio
targets.statement: For finite lists A,B and a unit q in a commutative ring, define the rational coefficient Qⱼ(A;B;q). For j≥0 it is Pⱼ(A;q)/Pⱼ(B;q); for j=−n<0 it is ∏_{j=1}^n∏_{b∈B}(1−bq^(−j))/∏_{a∈A}(1−aq^(−j)). Only the denominator in the appropriate expression must be a unit. This is the regular continuation of a quotient, even where an individual negative-index P for B has a pole.
hypotheses: Every denominator factor used for the chosen index is a unit; q a unit

targets.name: formalQPochhammer
targets.statement: For any commutative ring K and a∈K, define P̂(a;X)∈K⟦X⟧ by the coefficientwise limit ∏_{j≥0}(1−aXʲ). The factor at j=0 is retained. Define its positive tail P̂₊(a;X)=∏_{j≥1}(1−aXʲ), a unit with constant coefficient 1. Parameter families live in native polynomial or Laurent-polynomial coefficient rings; completion is in X only.
hypotheses: K commutative ring; coefficientwise eventual stabilization; inverses only of P̂₊ or other proved units

locator.where: (1.2.7), p. 3, line 127; formal interpretation via Pak2002 §2.2.1, line 442; Gasper1995 line 127

proofSketch: Every positive factor first changes degree j; form each coefficient using the stabilized finite product. Apply the native power-series unit criterion and supplier scalar-change theorem.

targets.name: qPochhammer_calculus
targets.statement: For every commutative ring, Pₙ₊ₘ(a;q)=Pₙ(a;q)Pₘ(aqⁿ;q). If a and q are units, Pₙ(a;q)=(−a)ⁿq^(n(n−1)/2)Pₙ(a⁻¹;q⁻¹). Integer-index versions hold on the common reciprocal-factor domain. These identities, including list multiplicities, commute with scalar change.
hypotheses: n,m≥0; a,q units only for inversion; reciprocal factors units for negative indices

locator.where: (1.3.10) and Exercise 1.1(ii), pp. 6–7, lines 313 and 327; Gasper1995 line 313

targets.name: qPochhammer_limit

The finite/infinite relation is P(a;q)=Pₙ(a;q)P(aqⁿ;q); division by the tail is stated only if that tail is nonzero.
hypotheses: a,q complex; |q|<1; an explicit nonzero-tail hypothesis when dividing

locator.where: (1.2.7) and Exercise 1.1(i), pp. 3, 7, lines 127 and 328; Gasper1995 line 127

layers.title: basic hypergeometric series on their actual domains

targets.name: basicHypergeometricPhi
targets.statement: For finite complex lists A,B of lengths r,s, define the unilateral coefficient cₙ=Pₙ(A;q)/Pₙ(q,B;q)·[(-1)^n q^(n(n−1)/2)]^(1+s−r) and Φ(A;B;q,z)=Σₙ≥0 cₙzⁿ whenever this is summable. Negative powers use nonzero q. A terminating numerator q^(−N) means the finite sum 0≤n≤N with denominators checked only on that range; no subsequent 0/0 is evaluated. The formal version is the coefficient sequence over the localization generated by its actual denominator factors.
hypotheses: All denominator factors nonzero; q≠0 if 1+s−r<0; a finite stopping bound supplied in the terminating case

locator.where: (3.1.6), p. 13, line 717; domain paragraph p. 14, line 761; Gasper1995 line 717

api.name: basicHypergeometricPhi_coeff
api.statement: The displayed normalized coefficient

tests.statement: For A=B=[], c₀=1 and c₁=−1/(1−q); omitting the normalization changes the sign.

tests.name: phiStopZero
tests.statement: A=[1] terminates at N=0 with value 1, even if a later denominator would vanish.

tests.name: phiBadDenominator

proofSketch: Construct coefficients first; use the finite product API for adjacent ratios and cancellations. Analytic values are paired with summability assertions, rather than treating tsum outside its domain as the function.

targets.name: basicHypergeometricPsi
targets.statement: For complex lists A,B with lengths r,s, q≠0 and z≠0, define Ψ by summing over j∈ℤ the terms Qⱼ(A;B;q)(−1)^((s−r)j)q^((s−r)j(j−1)/2)zʲ. The admissibility of Q is checked separately on each half-line. If a numerator parameter q^(−N) stops the positive tail, or a denominator parameter q^M with M≥1 stops the negative tail, use the resulting finite range with coefficients zero beyond its endpoint; denominator factors are checked only before stopping and no later 0/0 is evaluated. This quotient-based definition includes a vanishing negative tail when a denominator parameter equals a positive power of q.
hypotheses: q,z≠0; the Q denominator factors on each actual nonzero range are nonzero; explicit bounds for stopped tails; summability for infinite tails

api.name: basicHypergeometricPsi_split
api.statement: Separate j≥0 and j<0 using Q₋ₙ

api.name: basicHypergeometricPsi_shift
api.statement: Put h=s−r. For k∈ℤ on the common admissible, absolutely summable domain, Ψ(A;B;q,z)=Q_k(A;B;q)(−1)^(hk)q^(hk(k−1)/2)z^k Ψ(Aq^k;Bq^k;q,zq^(hk)); list scaling is entrywise.

tests.name: psiToPhi

tests.name: psiZeroArgument

proofSketch: Sum the explicitly normalized terms on ℤ and use the decomposition into nonnegative and negative integers. Clear denominators before relating Q to individual integer products.

targets.name: basicHypergeometric_convergence
targets.statement: For 0<|q|<1, a nonterminating Φ converges absolutely for all z if r≤s, for |z|<1 if r=s+1, and only at z=0 if r>s+1. For |q|>1 put r₀=#nonzero A, s₀=#nonzero B and d=s−r+r₀−s₀. The positive Φ tail has asymptotic ratio magnitude |z|·|∏A≠0/ (q∏B≠0)|·|q|^(dn): d<0 gives every z, d=0 gives |z|<|q∏B≠0/∏A≠0|, and d>0 gives only zero. For Ψ, its positive tail at |q|<1 has ratio |z|·|q|^((s−r)n), while its negative tail has ratio |∏B≠0/(z∏A≠0)|·|q|^(dn); at |q|>1 its positive tail has the latter degree d with reciprocal prefactor |z∏A≠0/∏B≠0| and its negative tail has ratio |z|⁻¹|q|^((s−r)n). Intersect the two strict ratio domains. Every eventually zero tail is finite and overrides its nonterminating classification; on a finite nonzero-radius boundary the nonterminating terms do not tend to zero. For q=0 and e=1+s−r≥0, put C=∏(1−a)/∏(1−b): Φ=1+Cz/(1−z) if e=0 and |z|<1, and Φ=1+(−1)^e Cz if e>0.
hypotheses: All actual denominators nonzero; nontermination for divergence claims; products of nonzero entries use empty product 1; q=0 case has e≥0

locator.where: pp. 14–15, lines 761–854; corrected |q|>1 radius by (1.3.10)–(1.3.11), lines 313–323; Gasper1995 line 761

The normalized bilateral j-th term equals Q_j(A⁻¹;B⁻¹;q⁻¹)·(z∏A/∏B)ʲ. These are term identities on the common denominator domain; summation requires both actual tails.

proofSketch: Use the exact adjacent-term ratios, taking degrees after deleting zero parameters only in the leading products. For the negative tail use Q₋ₙ. A convergent product of the residual 1+O(|q|^n) factors proves failure of termwise decay at a finite boundary. Compute q=0 directly.

targets.name: qBinomial_and_euler
targets.statement: For complex a, |q|<1 and |z|<1, Σₙ Pₙ(a;q)zⁿ/Pₙ(q;q)=P(az;q)/P(z;q). Consequently Σ zⁿ/Pₙ(q;q)=P(z;q)⁻¹ on |z|<1, and Σ q^(n(n−1)/2)zⁿ/Pₙ(q;q)=P(−z;q) for every complex z. For |q|>1 the binomial sum is P(z/q;q⁻¹)/P(az/q;q⁻¹) on |az/q|<1. Formal coefficient identities hold in K[A]⟦Q⟧⟦Z⟧ for every commutative ring K, with the q-products interpreted coefficientwise in Q and Z and all denominators units.
hypotheses: Complex domains as stated; for the formal statement Q and Z are independent indeterminates; every analytic denominator is proved nonzero on its stated domain

The quotient-coefficient formulation includes b=q^N, N≥1, by its vanishing negative tail and analytic continuation.
hypotheses: a,z,q≠0; Pₙ(b;q)≠0 for n≥0; Pₙ(aq^(−n);q)≠0 for n≥1; infinite denominator factors nonzero; annulus inequality

targets.name: baileyPair
targets.statement: For a commutative ring K with all Pₙ(q;q) and Pₙ(aq;q) specified units, a Bailey pair relative to (a,q) is a pair of sequences α,β:ℕ→K satisfying βₙ=Σ_{r=0}^n αᵣ/(Pₙ₋ᵣ(q;q)Pₙ₊ᵣ(aq;q)). This is a linear relation, so normalization α₀=β₀=1 is a separate condition, not a requirement on every pair.
hypotheses: K commutative ring; every denominator in the displayed relation is a specified unit

locator.where: Bailey’s Lemma (2.3), p. 114, lines 85–108; Andrews1986 line 85

targets.name: baileyLemma
targets.statement: For a Bailey pair (α,β), units ρ₁,ρ₂ and t=aq/(ρ₁ρ₂), define α′ₙ=Pₙ(ρ₁,ρ₂;q)tⁿαₙ/Pₙ(aq/ρ₁,aq/ρ₂;q) and β′ₙ=Σ_{j=0}^n Pⱼ(ρ₁,ρ₂;q)Pₙ₋ⱼ(t;q)tʲβⱼ/(Pₙ₋ⱼ(q;q)Pₙ(aq/ρ₁,aq/ρ₂;q)). Then (α′,β′) is a Bailey pair. Over ℂ, for |q|<1, |t|<1, all stated denominator products nonzero, and Σ|αₙtⁿ|<∞, the identity Σ Pₙ(ρ₁,ρ₂;q)tⁿβₙ=P(aq/ρ₁,aq/ρ₂;q)/P(aq,t;q)·Σ Pₙ(ρ₁,ρ₂;q)tⁿαₙ/Pₙ(aq/ρ₁,aq/ρ₂;q) holds absolutely. For the same complex Bailey pair, assume |q|<1 and P(aq;q)≠0. The two-parameter limit is Σ aⁿq^(n²)βₙ=P(aq;q)⁻¹Σ aⁿq^(n²)αₙ under Σ|aⁿq^(n²)αₙ|<∞. For fixed ρ≠0 with P(aq/ρ;q)≠0, the one-parameter limit is Σ Pₙ(ρ;q)(−aq/ρ)ⁿq^(n(n−1)/2)βₙ=P(aq/ρ;q)/P(aq;q)·Σ Pₙ(ρ;q)(−aq/ρ)ⁿq^(n(n−1)/2)αₙ/Pₙ(aq/ρ;q), under Σ|(−aq/ρ)ⁿq^(n(n−1)/2)αₙ|<∞. Both equalities assert absolute convergence. They are the termwise ρ₁,ρ₂→∞ and ρ₁→∞ specializations, proved directly from the finite Bailey relation with these bounds. (Andrews1986, Bailey’s Lemma (2.3)–(2.6), pp. 114–115, lines 93–110; limiting identity (3.1), p. 116; Andrews1986 line 93.)
hypotheses: All finite denominator factors are units; ρ₁,ρ₂ units; analytic hypotheses as stated; no denominator cancellation through zero
For both limiting sums: |q|<1, P(aq;q)≠0; the specified weighted α-series is absolutely summable; for the one-parameter limit ρ≠0 and P(aq/ρ;q)≠0

proofSketch: Substitute the finite β relation, exchange the finite triangular sums, and clear all supplied unit denominators. The remaining finite kernel identity follows by q-Pascal induction, including the n=0 boundary; it gives the new pair relation. For the infinite formula take n→∞ in both expressions for β′ₙ. layers.title: polynomial identities and partition-series adapters

targets.name: gaussianPolynomial
targets.statement: Define G(n,k)∈ℤ[Q] as the generating polynomial of partitions whose diagram fits inside a k by (n−k) rectangle, for 0≤k≤n, and zero outside that range, including signed integer k<0. Equivalently its Q-exponent enumerates k-element subsets of {0,…,n−1} by sum minus k(k−1)/2. Evaluate this integral polynomial in every commutative ring.
hypotheses: n≥0; k integral; coefficient ring commutative; no division

locator.where: (1.3.3)–(1.3.4), pp. 5–6, lines 267–284; rectangle interpretation is the finite-subset derivation; Gasper1995 line 267

targets.name: schur_finiteIdentities

Terms with j>n or invalid lower Gaussian index are zero; thus both displayed sums are finite.
hypotheses: n natural; G has the out-of-range convention of 3.1; exponents computed in integers before conversion to naturals

locator.where: (4.2.11)–(4.2.12), p. 29, line 1672; finite identities are the author’s Pascal derivation of these endpoints; Gasper1995 line 1672

targets.name: rankCrankDissections
targets.statement: For a primitive ℓth root ζ and |q|<1, construct the complete identities R(ζ;q)=Σ_{r=0}^{ℓ−1}qʳD^R_(ℓ,r)(q^ℓ) for ℓ=5,7 and V(ζ;q)=Σ_{r=0}^{ℓ−1}qʳD^V_(ℓ,r)(q^ℓ) for ℓ=5,7,11. The coefficient of Xⁿ in D^R is Σ_a ζ^a N(a,ℓ,ℓn+r), and the analogous signed vector count gives D^V. Identify every D with its theta-product and, for rank, Lambert-series expression, not only its zero classes. The rank expressions are the complete rank-difference identities of AtkinSwinnertonDyer1954 pp. 84–106, with the empty partition convention of §4.3; the crank expressions are Garvan1988 (3.1), (5.2), (6.8) and their product definitions (3.4)–(3.7), (5.3), (6.1)–(6.14). In particular put J_(a,m)(X)=P(X^a,X^(m−a),X^m;X^m), E(X)=P(X;X), A=J_(2,5)/P(X,X^4;X^5)², B=E(X^5)/P(X,X^4;X^5), C=E(X^5)/P(X²,X³;X^5), D=J_(1,5)/P(X²,X³;X^5)². Then V(ζ₅;q)=A(q⁵)−(ζ₅+ζ₅⁻¹)²qB(q⁵)+(ζ₅²+ζ₅⁻²)q²C(q⁵)−(ζ₅+ζ₅⁻¹)q³D(q⁵). The D-functions are analytic on the disc and all sums used to obtain them are absolutely summable there. Prove D^R_(5,4)=D^R_(7,5)=D^V_(5,4)=D^V_(7,5)=D^V_(11,6)=0. (Garvan1988, §§2–6, (3.1), (3.4)–(3.7), Theorems (5.1), (6.7), lines 419–443, 609–627, 687–708; rank: AtkinSwinnertonDyer1954 pp. 84–106; rank-five comparison Garvan1988 §8.) For the complete seven-dissection, put c_j=ζ₇ʲ+ζ₇^(−j), U(X)=P(X,X²,X⁵,X⁶;X⁷)⁻¹, V₇(X)=P(X,X³,X⁴,X⁶;X⁷)⁻¹ and W(X)=P(X²,X³,X⁴,X⁵;X⁷)⁻¹. The ordered tuple (D^V_(7,r))_(r=0,…,6) is E(X)·(U²,(c₁−1)UV₇,c₂V₇²,(c₃+1)UW,−c₁V₇W,0,−(c₂+1)W²), all functions evaluated at X. For eleven put c_j=ζ₁₁ʲ+ζ₁₁^(−j), Q_b=J_(b,33)(X), (A₀,A₃,A₇,A₈,A₉)=(Q₁₅,Q₁₂,Q₆,Q₃,Q₉), and (B₀,B₁,B₂,B₄,B₇)=(Q₁₆−X²Q₅,Q₁₄−XQ₈,Q₁₃−X³Q₂,Q₇+XQ₄,Q₁₀+X³Q₁). Then E(X)·(D^V_(11,r))_(r=0,…,10) equals (A₀B₀−X³A₇B₄, (c₁−1)(A₀B₁−X⁴A₈B₄), c₂(A₀B₂−X²A₉B₄), (c₃+1)(A₃B₀−X²A₇B₇), (c₂+c₄+1)(A₃B₁−X³A₈B₇), −(c₂+c₄)(A₃B₂−XA₈B₇), 0, (c₁+c₄)(A₀B₇−XA₃B₄), −(c₂+c₅+1)X(A₇B₁−XA₈B₀), −(c₄+1)(A₉B₀−XA₇B₂), −c₃(A₉B₁−X²A₈B₂)). Cyclotomic Galois transport gives these identities for every primitive root, not just exp(2πi/ℓ). (Garvan1988 Theorems (5.1), (6.7), lines 609–627, 687–708.) For rank, put Δ_(a,r)(X)=Σ_{n≥0}(N(a,ℓ,ℓn+r)−N(0,ℓ,ℓn+r))Xⁿ. The complete rank target is D^R_(ℓ,r)=Σ_{a=1}^{ℓ−1}ζ^aΔ_(a,r) for every 0≤r<ℓ, together with the product/Lambert evaluations of every Δ in AtkinSwinnertonDyer1954 pp. 84–106. This identity fixes the interface without adding the ordinary partition term, since Σ_{a=0}^{ℓ−1}ζ^a=0. The Lambert terms in the nonzero rank residues remain part of the target.
hypotheses: ζ primitive; |q|<1; rank ℓ=5,7; vector crank ℓ=5,7,11; denominators are positive Euler factors and hence nonzero

targets.statement: Construct the following integral modules with finite supports, independently of partition divisibility. For ℓ=5,7 use x=e(τ), B=xP(x²⁴;x²⁴)=η(24τ), C=x^ℓP(x^(24ℓ);x^(24ℓ))=η(24ℓτ), b_j=Cʲ/B^(j+1), and Ω_ℓ(Σ a_nxⁿ)=Σ a_(ℓn)xⁿ on Laurent series bounded below. Put O₅=span_ℤ{5^(5n)b_(12n+5),5^(5n+2)b_(12n+11)} and E₅=span_ℤ{5^(5n)b_(12n+6),5^(5n+3)b_(12n+12)} for n≥0. Prove Ω₅O₅⊆5E₅, Ω₅E₅⊆5O₅ and Ω₅(B⁻¹)=5b₅. Put E₇=span_ℤ{7^(7n)b_(16n+4),7^(7n+2)b_(16n+8),7^(7n+3)b_(16n+12),7^(7n+5)b_(16n+16)} and O₇=span_ℤ{7^(7n)b_(16n+3),7^(7n+2)b_(16n+7),7^(7n+4)b_(16n+11),7^(7n+6)b_(16n+15)}. Prove Ω₇E₇⊆O₇, Ω₇O₇⊆7E₇, Ω₇(B⁻¹)=7b₃+49b₇ and Ω₇²(B⁻¹)∈49E₇. The first seven-step is separate: Ω₇(B⁻¹)/7 need not lie in O₇. Transport these estimates to §4.8 by L_r(x²⁴)=CΩ_ℓʳ(B⁻¹) for odd r and BΩ_ℓʳ(B⁻¹) for even r. All b_j used have integral Laurent expansions since the Euler tails are units; their eta weights and multipliers are retained. For ℓ=11 use the modular-function basis below, rather than an eta-power basis on the genus-one curve. (Watson1938, §3 (3.2), (3.21)–(3.23), (3.41)–(3.44), pp. 105–110, lines 409–698; §5 (5.2), (5.21)–(5.23), (5.41)–(5.42), pp. 118–122, lines 1081–1390; Atkin1967 Lemmas 3–8, 11–14 and Appendix A, lines 95–121, 232–247, 414–484, 514–565.) For the level-11 module, let G₂,G₃ be functions on Γ₀(11), holomorphic on ℍ, with only a pole at infinity, vanishing at cusp 0, and principal parts q⁻²+2q⁻¹ and q⁻³−3q⁻²−5q⁻¹ respectively. Existence and uniqueness are part of `etaDecimationModules_basis`. Set G₄=G₂²−11G₃, G₅=(η(τ)/η(11τ))¹², G₆=G₂G₄, and G_(n+5)=G_nG₅ for n≥2. For n=5a+r, r=2,3,4,5,6, put θ(n)=6a+(2,3,4,6,6)_r and g_n=11^(−θ(n))G_n(−1/(11τ)). Set ξ(2)=0, ξ(3)=1 and ξ(5a+r)=5a+(1,3,3,4,5)_r for r=4,5,6,7,8; set ε(2)=0, ε(3)=1 and ε(n)=ξ(n)+1 for n≥4. Define X₁₁=span_ℤ{11^ξ(n)g_n:n≥2}, Y₁₁=span_ℤ{11^ε(n)g_n:n≥2}. Prove integral Fourier embeddings, U₁₁X₁₁⊆11Y₁₁, U₁₁(φ₁₁Y₁₁)⊆11X₁₁ and U₁₁φ₁₁∈11X₁₁. These are Atkin1967 Lemmas 3, 7, 13 and the base step at lines 481–484; Lemmas 8, 14 retain the unit leading-coordinate refinement. The basis has distinct orders at infinity 5a+(1,2,3,5,4)_r for r=2,3,4,5,6, so its finite expansions are unique.

Write the matrix as g=[[a,b],[c,dγ]] to distinguish its entry dγ from the characteristic difference d. On the stabilizer write (α,β)g=(α+k,β+l), (γ,δ)g=(γ+m,δ+n). Write the unreduced transformed differences as d′τ+e′, the B-differences as d_Bτ+e_B, K=d′−d_B and L=e′−e_B. targets.name: realAnalyticModularSpace
targets.statement: For a finite-index subgroup Γ of Mp₂(ℤ), a finite-dimensional complex representation ρ and k∈(1/2)ℤ, define the space A_k(Γ,ρ) of real-analytic functions F:ℍ→V with F(γτ)=φγ(τ)^(2k)ρ(γ)F(τ). Define exponential cusp growth by requiring each normalized slash F|_k δ to be O(exp(Cy)), uniformly over a cusp period, for every rational cusp δ∞. For arbitrary ρ the cusp slash is φδ(τ)^(−2k)F(δτ), with the representation transported to δ⁻¹Γδ; it does not evaluate ρ on δ outside its domain. When ρ extends to Mp₂(ℤ), applying the additional constant factor ρ(δ)⁻¹ gives an equivalent growth condition. Define weakly holomorphic, holomorphic and cusp subspaces by holomorphy on ℍ and finite principal parts, nonnegative exponents and vanishing constant terms in the corresponding cusp expansions. Scalar multiplier spaces are the one-dimensional instances; conjugate representations are always allowed and duals are identified only with an invariant Hermitian form. (BruinierFunke2003, §3, pp. 8–10, lines 366–374 and 461–470; Zagier2009 §5, lines 640–677; BruinierFunke2003 line 366.)

Finite principal parts allow finitely many negative real exponents; holomorphic cusp data have none and are bounded at real exponent zero, while cusp data tend to zero. targets.name: parabolicFourierExpansion
targets.statement: Let V be finite dimensional over ℂ, Γ≤Mp₂(ℤ) finite index, ρ:Γ→GL(V), and k∈(1/2)ℤ. At a cusp choose a positive width w with the lift (T^w,1) in the transported subgroup, and let M be its action. Choose the matrix logarithm A with exp(2πiA)=M, scalar eigenvalues λ satisfying 0≤Re(λ)<1 and the nilpotent logarithm on each generalized eigenspace. For a real-analytic harmonic cusp slash f with f(τ+w)=Mf(τ) and uniform exponential growth, write f(x+iy)=Σ_n exp(2πiB_n x)v_n(y), B_n=(nI+A)/w. Prove locally uniform convergence with derivatives through order two and the matrix ODE v_n″+(k/y)v_n′+((2πk/y)B_n−4π²B_n²)v_n=0. On each generalized eigenspace of B_n with eigenvalue β, every mode is uniquely exp(−2πB_n y)a_n+K_(k,B_n)(y)b_n, where K_(k,B)(y)=exp(−2πBy)J_(k,B)(y), J_(k,B)(y)=−∫_y^∞t^(−k)exp(4πBt)dt if Re(β)<0 and J_(k,B)(y)=∫_1^y t^(−k)exp(4πBt)dt if Re(β)≥0. The negative-frequency integral converges because its exponential decay dominates all Jordan polynomials. The two resulting Fourier parts converge on every compact subset of ℍ; growth makes all sufficiently positive-frequency b_n and sufficiently negative-frequency a_n vanish. This gives normalized parts, using decay at infinity on negative frequencies and base height 1 on the remaining modes; for real β≠0, H_k(2πβy)=−(−4πβ)^(1−k)K_(k,β)(y)+δ_(β>0)H_k(2πβ)exp(−2πβ(y−1)), using §8.4’s branch. At β=0 and k≠1, y^(1−k)=(1−k)K_(k,0)(y)+1. For holomorphic slashes b_n=0 and exp(2πiB_nτ) has polynomial τ-factors on Jordan blocks. Finite principal parts, holomorphy and vanishing at a cusp mean respectively finitely many exponents with negative real part, none with negative real part, and convergence to zero; polynomial factors on the Re(exponent)=0 boundary must satisfy the stated boundedness or vanishing condition. No unitary or semisimplicity hypothesis is imposed. At k=1 the integral at B_n=0 is log y; no k=1 surjectivity is asserted. (KnoppMason2009, arXiv v1 §2.2, Lemma 2.1, Theorem 2.2 and Lemma 2.3, pp. 4–6, lines 188–241, for holomorphic logarithmic expansions; harmonic extension by the displayed ODE from §8.2 and reduction of order as in BruinierFunke2003 lines 395–423.)

targets.statement: For every nondegenerate even integral lattice L, every k∈(1/2)ℤ with k≠1, every finite-index Γ≤Mp₂(ℤ), and F∈H_k(Γ,ρ_L), each cusp expansion decomposes uniquely into F⁺+F⁻ using exp(−w), H_k(w), and the constant pair 1,y^(1−k). At infinity for the full group, n∈ℤ+Q(h), h∈L∨/L, F⁺=Σ a⁺(h,n)e(nτ)e_h and F⁻=Σ_h[a⁻(h,0)y^(1−k)+Σ_{n≠0}a⁻(h,n)H_k(2πny)e(nx)]e_h. Only finitely many negative a⁺ and positive a⁻ occur. ξ_k maps H onto a subspace of M!_{2−k}(Γ,ρ_{L−}); its kernel is exactly M!_k. On H⁺ the n≥0 nonholomorphic coefficients vanish at each cusp, and ξ is cuspidal. (BruinierFunke2003, (3.2), Lemmas 3.1, 3.3–3.4, Proposition 3.2, H⁺ definition, pp. 9–11, lines 384–515; ambient dimension assumption §2 line 190; BruinierFunke2003 line 384.)
hypotheses: L even integral nondegenerate of any signature; k∈(1/2)ℤ and k≠1; Γ finite index; growth at every cusp; ρ_L is the positive-T Weil convention from §4.7
ρ_L=conj(ω_L), finiteWeil_conjugate of MetaplecticAutomorphicForms §4.7; positive T exponent

locator.where: (3.2), Lemmas 3.1, 3.3–3.4, Proposition 3.2, H⁺ definition, pp. 9–11, lines 384–515; ambient dimension assumption §2 line 190; BruinierFunke2003 line 384

proofSketch: Diagonalize the finite-order cusp translation supplied by the Weil representation and recover coefficients by period integration. The harmonic equation gives 8.4’s scalar ODE. Growth and the two asymptotics cut off the forbidden tails. Apply L and conjugate to compute ξ; the constant and nonzero modes prove kernel equality and the cusp-shadow characterization. Transport every step to each cusp. The coefficient bounds follow from the modular small-y bound and circle integration, as in Lemmas 3.3–3.4, lines 503–515. Bruinier–Funke §2 line 190 assumes ambient dimension at least 3; first add two even unimodular hyperbolic planes and transport the unchanged discriminant representation to justify all smaller ranks, including rank zero.

The sequences 0→M!_k→H_k→M!_{2−k}→0 and 0→M!_k→H_k⁺→S_{2−k}→0 are exact as real vector spaces, or as complex spaces after conjugating the last term. This holds for every finite-index Γ and k≠1; it is not a surjectivity assertion for an arbitrary representation.
hypotheses: Exactly the even-lattice, half-integral k≠1 and all-cusp hypotheses of 8.5; no weight or signature narrowing

proofSketch: Pass to a normal torsion-free finite-index subgroup. The vector-bundle Dolbeault and Serre-duality contract gives H¹(E(nD))=0 for large cusp divisor nD and solves ∂bar F=(i/2)y^(−k)conj(g)dbarτ with pole bounds: subtract cutoff local Fourier primitives at the cusps first, then solve the compactly supported remaining forcing. The factor i/2 is fixed by 8.2’s xi normalization. Holomorphy of g implies ΔF=0. Average over the finite quotient to descend; restrict to inverse images of cusp forms for the second sequence. ModularForms 10B supplies the line-bundle cohomology foundation; the recorded Part II contract supplies the required vector-bundle extension.

targets.name: mockModularForm
targets.statement: A mock modular form is a holomorphic part h with a specified normalized nonholomorphic Fourier correction F⁻ such that F=h+F⁻ belongs to H_k(Γ,ρ); its shadow is ξ_k F, required to be holomorphic at every cusp in the standard mock space. The full space H_k, with weakly holomorphic shadows that may have cusp poles, remains a separate harmonic Maass space. Include the completion and its cusp-coordinate normalization in the object, rather than asserting a choice-free shadow for an arbitrary holomorphic function. For general ρ use the conjugate representation; with an invariant Hermitian structure identify it with the dual. Supply the scalar and vector, subgroup restriction, direct sum and intertwining-map APIs. On finite Weil modules use 8.5’s normalized parts; on general cusp monodromy use §8.4a’s decaying-negative-frequency and height-one normalization. (Zagier2009, §5, pp. 986–12–14, lines 640–735; BruinierFunke2003 (3.2), lines 423–438; Zagier2009 line 640.)
hypotheses: Holomorphic h on ℍ; actual harmonic completion with all-cusp exponential growth; prescribed normalized Fourier correction; k≠1 for use of 8.5, general k for the completion definition
Standard mock shadows are holomorphic at all cusps; their normalized corrections include the constant shadow term

locator.where: §5, pp. 986–12–14, lines 640–735; BruinierFunke2003 (3.2), lines 423–438; Zagier2009 line 640

proofSketch: Use §8.5 or §8.4a with the fixed logarithm, negative-frequency decay and remaining base height to normalize the correction. The injectivity of ∂bar on the normalized nonholomorphic modes proves shadow=0 iff F⁻=0; xi-kernel equality then gives weak holomorphy of F=h. The example F=conj(j−744) at weight 0 shows why polar shadows are excluded from that assertion. For a cusp shadow, differentiate the convergent Eichler integral at its moving lower endpoint: ∂bar F⁻=(i/2)y^(−k)conj(g), hence ξF⁻=g. Match its Fourier coefficients termwise; nonzero constant shadow uses the explicit y^(1−k) term instead of this cusp integral. The integral formula’s constant and orientation are verified by this derivative calculation.

Transport the positive-index theta decomposition of MetaplecticAutomorphicForms §6.20 through its classical-coordinate specialization: fix integral weight k, positive index m, trivial finite multiplier, the rank-one elliptic lattice and normal Fourier convergence, and impose holomorphy and cusp growth when comparing the holomorphic subspaces. Include the finite Weil convention. (Zwegers2002, (3.1)–(3.4), pp. 49–50, lines 2673–2696; Zwegers2002 line 2673.)

targets.name: meromorphicJacobiDatum
targets.statement: For positive integral m and integral k, a meromorphic elliptic datum is a function φ(z;τ) meromorphic in z for each τ∈ℍ, with φ(z+λτ+μ;τ)=exp(−2πim(λ²τ+2λz))φ(z;τ) for every pair of integers λ,μ off its poles. Define its modular subspace by φ(z/(cτ+d);γτ)=(cτ+d)^k exp(2πimcz²/(cτ+d))φ(z;τ). Pole sets, Laurent orders and principal parts use the native meromorphic germ carrier. Poles modulo Λτ form a finite set; no regularity in τ beyond what an individual analytic corollary needs is hidden in this pointwise decomposition datum. (Zwegers2002, §3.1 conditions (E),(M), p. 49, lines 2660–2668; Theorem 3.9, line 3101; Zwegers2002 line 2660.)
hypotheses: m≥1; k integral for the modular law; φ meromorphic in z; every equality evaluated off polar divisors

targets.name: realAnalyticMeromorphicResidue
targets.statement: For a meromorphic germ g at u with pole order at most s≥1, and a real-analytic germ f, define Res^RA_u(fg)=(1/(s−1)!)∂_v^(s−1)[f(v)(v−u)^s g(v)] at u. Equivalently this is the coefficient of (v−u)^(−1)conj(v−u)^0 in the mixed Laurent–Taylor expansion. Prove independence of s and affine coordinate covariance of the 1-form f(v)g(v)dv, including its Jacobian factor, for the coordinate changes used by Jacobi transformations. For holomorphic f it equals the ordinary residue.
hypotheses: s≥1 bounds the pole order of g; (v−u)^s g(v) extends holomorphically; f real analytic; ∂v is the holomorphic Wirtinger derivative

targets.name: completedJacobiPolarKernel
targets.statement: For m≥1, τ∈ℍ and z−u∉Λτ define f_m,u(z;τ)=Σ_{λ∈ℤ}exp(2πimλ²τ+4πimλz)/(1−e(λτ+z−u)). Define R_m,l(u;τ)=Σ_{λ≡l (mod 2m)}[sgn(λ+1/2)−E((λ+2m Im(u)/y)√(y/m))]exp(−πiλ²τ/(2m)−2πiλu), and fHat=f−(1/2)Σ_l R_m,l(u)θ_m,l(z). Prove normal convergence and smoothness off the poles. As a function of z, fHat is meromorphic with residue −1/(2πi) at z=u and satisfies the index-m elliptic law. Its u-shift is fHat_{u+λτ+μ}=exp(2πim(λ²τ+2λu))fHat_u. Under γ, fHat_{u/(cτ+d)}(z/(cτ+d);γτ)=(cτ+d)exp(2πimc(z²−u²)/(cτ+d))fHat_u(z;τ).
hypotheses: m positive integer; τ∈ℍ; z−u outside Λτ; all u complex

targets.name: meromorphicJacobi_decomposition
targets.statement: For every datum φ of 9.2 and every τ∈ℍ, choose p whose parallelogram P_p=p+(0,1)τ+(0,1) has no boundary poles. Put h_l(τ)=exp(−πil²τ/(2m))∫_p^{p+1}φ(v;τ)exp(−2πilv)dv−πiΣ_{u∈P_p∩poles}Res^RA_{v=u}[R_m,l(v;τ)φ(v;τ)]. These h_l are independent of p. For z outside the poles, φ(z;τ)=Σ_{l mod 2m}h_l(τ)θ_m,l(z;τ)−2πiΣ_{u mod Λτ}Res^RA_{v=u}[fHat_m,v(z;τ)φ(v;τ)]. If φ obeys the modular law of weight k, then h_l(τ+1)=exp(−πil²/(2m))h_l(τ) and h_l(−1/τ)=τ^k/(√(−iτ)√(2m))Σ_{ν mod 2m}exp(πilν/m)h_ν(τ).

proofSketch: Integrate the meromorphic uncompleted f_m,v(z)φ(v) around the pole-free boundary. Opposite edges give the theta integrals using the inhomogeneous u-shift. The residue theorem supplies all principal-part derivatives. Substituting fHat cancels exactly half the R-theta terms and gives the displayed coefficient correction. Contour movement plus 9.3 proves independence of p; kernel covariance proves S and T. No harmonicity claim is attached to arbitrary h_l.

For τ∈ℍ put F₃=(q^(−1/24)f(q),2q^(1/3)ω(q^(1/2)),2q^(1/3)ω(−q^(1/2))), where fractional q-powers mean exp(2πirτ).

It is harmonic of weight 1/2, has all-cusp exponential growth, and ξH₃=−2√6·conj((g₁,g₀,−g₂)(−conj τ)). G₃ is bounded on vertical approach to every rational cusp.
